title: Warping, layering, and color grading in Photoshop: two-image landscape blends (ESDV Images and blends)
summary: This video walks through a Photoshop-driven workflow for landscape blending using two images, focusing on composition via warps, depth separation with selective blur, and sky/foreground color grading. The presenter demonstrates perspective and puppet warps to resize and reshape foreground elements, then blends warped results back into the original using history brushes. A series of RAW adjustments, color grading, and selective color work follows to sculpt mood, depth, and tonal separation, culminating in a Milky Way composite that blends two exposures with cloning, diffusion, and horizon glow. Throughout, the emphasis is on preserving a believable scene while achieving three-dimensional depth and a strong visual lead toward the subject.

sections.title: Intro: focus stacking note, crop decision, and two warp concepts
sections.description: The presenter recalls two images were aligned via focus stacking, but one was cropped/warped and thus not stacked. The plan is to demonstrate two main edits: sky color enhancement and warping to adjust composition.

sections.title: Perspective Warp introduction: establishing regions and three-box workflow
sections.description: The first warp type shown is Perspective Warp, splitting the scene into regions (mountains/Joshua trees vs. top of trees). The presenter explains limiting to typical three boxes (sometimes more) and demonstrates how warping reshapes size and proportion to improve composition.

sections.title: Puppet Warp and selective warping: pin placement and masking
sections.description: A shift to Puppet Warp shows dense meshes for fine control. The speaker demonstrates dropping a warp pin around a cloud, locking corners, and stretching only the target area. They emphasize blending the warp back into the original with the history brush to avoid unintended changes elsewhere.

sections.title: Depth management and sky color refinement via RAW and local painting
sections.description: Background blur is introduced as a depth cue to push the background farther away. The RAW editor is used to boost sky color (temperature/tint) and then a selective painting approach (via history brush) helps apply adjustments to specific elements (clouds first, then blending back).

sections.title: Cactus glow with color shifts and edge painting
sections.description: A big curves adjustment increases cactus glow; yellow and orange hues are refined in HSL and saturation is increased. Edges are painted to emphasize glow while preserving natural edges; the emphasis remains on controlled, localized color to avoid oversaturation.

sections.title: Two-exposure blending, straightening, and sky composition
sections.description: The speaker shifts to tilt correction for a sun-star image, then explains how to blend two exposures (foreground/mid-ground vs sky) using a clone-stamp workflow to align and merge. The method aims to preserve a believable horizon while increasing depth and color separation. The process includes selecting regions, blending, and matching exposure between layers.

sections.title: Milky Way composition: dehaze, selective color, blur, and horizon glow
sections.description: The final major section focuses on Milky Way processing: creating tonal separation between foreground and sky, separating sky colors using dehaze, selective color, and color balance, and applying a horizon glow using a blur that diffuses distant elements. The guide then shows painting the foreground back in where needed and using cloning/edge-control to maintain separation and realism. The presenter notes the difference between 'real' vs 'fake' Milky Way composites and demonstrates a method to blend the galactic core with a believable horizon glow.
